canberra.title: Accused mall attacker allegedly pretends to be a car then ‘runs over’ children
canberra.snippet: The young man accused of attacking two boys inside a Canberra mall allegedly pretends to be a car before he “runs over” child...
canberra.content:
23 September 2026

An 18-year-old man allegedly assaulted two children at Westfield Belconnen on 14 August 2026. Photo: Westfield Belconnen Facebook, Michelle Kroll, Albert McKnight.

The young man accused of attacking two boys inside a Canberra mall allegedly pretends to be a car before he “runs over” children, a court has heard.

The two boys, aged two and four, were with their mother at Westfield Belconnen on 14 August 2026 when they were allegedly attacked by an 18-year-old male stranger.

One child was allegedly kicked, while the younger boy was reportedly left with a broken nose.

The 18-year-old man, whose name has been legally suppressed, was refused bail several days later. During the hearing, the ACT Magistrates Court heard of his extensive disabilities and prior allegations that he had assaulted multiple children in public.

The man spent about a month in custody before beginning his second bail application last week, which continued on Wednesday (23 September).

The court was closed for a time while the man’s mother gave evidence. When it reopened, the court heard that the man apparently had the intellectual capacity of a 10-year-old.

“He doesn’t belong in a prison,” Special Magistrate Sean Richter said.

“However, how can I/we protect the community in the meantime, when the behaviour is that he pretends he’s a car and runs over small children?”

The court had previously heard that the man’s father apparently told police his son “thinks he is a car and is causing car accidents with the children”.

Special Magistrate Richter was concerned the man may seriously injure a child or a child’s parent may seriously injure him if he were in the community.

“He may find himself in a confrontation with an incredibly angry parent,” he said.

The special magistrate said he did not think the man’s mother could control her son, who he thought had to deal with a “very, very difficult situation”.

“He impulsively goes off … He runs and runs and runs,” he said.

Special Magistrate Richter did question what would happen to the case, because the man appeared to have the intellectual capacity of a 10-year-old and the ACT had raised the age of criminal responsibility to 14.

The man’s lawyer, Gillian Bilton of Legal Aid, said the charges would take a long time to progress through the courts and she was concerned that if her client were refused bail, he would spend a very long period on remand.

Special Magistrate Richter wanted to hear from the man’s father. He also encouraged the family to install alarms and locks on their doors, then take photos as proof for the court.

The bail application was adjourned again to continue on Monday (28 September).

Before adjourning, the special magistrate did say he didn’t want to see the man in custody.

“I can’t think of a worse place for a boy with this disability to be other than the AMC [Alexander Maconochie Centre],” he said.

The man has been charged with two counts of assault. No pleas have been entered.

canberra.title: Government rejects claims public specialist school funding will be cut
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government says Canberra’s specialist schools will not have their budgets cut despite figures showing multimillion-dollar r...
canberra.content:
Education Directorate director-general Jo Wood said specialist schools knew their bottom lines wouldn’t be changing. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

The ACT Government says Canberra’s specialist schools will not have their budgets cut despite figures showing multimillion-dollar reductions under the new school budgeting model.

Figures reported today suggest Malkara Specialist School would lose more than $2.8 million, Black Mountain School more than $3 million, Cranleigh School more than $1.7 million and The Woden School more than $1.6 million from their 2026-27 budgets.

But Education Directorate director-general Jo Wood said those figures represented the schools’ Student Resource Allocation (SRA), not their total funding.

She said there shouldn’t be any confusion about what specialist schools were receiving.

“We’re communicating directly with specialist schools – including in writing – so I believe our special school principals do understand that the SRA [student resource allocation] isn’t their funding, it’s SRA plus additional funding based on their needs,” she said.

“We estimate that special schools, across the four, will have an additional $7 million beyond their SRA for 2027.”

The clarification comes as the ACT Government faces growing criticism over the rollout of a new funding model for public schools, with principals, parents and the Opposition questioning what the changes will mean for staffing and services.

The ACT’s public schools operated under an autonomous model, meaning each institution controlled its budgets and other administrative tasks.

But an independent review into public school resourcing called for a centralised system to ease administrative burdens, avoid duplication, save time and money, and achieve a fairer distribution of staff and resources.

This includes deciding budgets through School Resource Allocation funding plus adjustment-based resourcing funding for students with extra needs.

Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith previously said overall public school funding had been boosted by 7.3 per cent since 2025-26, and stated 43 schools had draft funding within the plus-or-minus 5 per cent variance, 31 would see a more than 5 per cent increase, and 18 will lose more than 5 per cent of their previous budgets.

On Wednesday (23 September), she said the government had been clear from the start that the SRA model wouldn’t be applied to specialist schools.

“There was a separate conversation around specialist schools to ensure that they are not going to lose funding from the 26-27 school year, so that absolutely needs to be clear,” Ms Stephen-Smith said.

“We recognise that specialist schools are in a different situation and that the the student resourcing allocation model doesn’t really work for those schools when it comes to their budgets.”

Ms Stephen-Smith was also adamant that the budgets presented to the ACT’s public school principals weren’t set in stone, and the government was willing to talk.

“I recognise that conversation’s been really difficult and that communication probably could have been better. Timelines were very, very tight for principals.

“It’s been a complex process; it’s the first time that we’ve done school budgets in this way, and so we’ve learnt through the process as well.

“We’re nowhere near the end of that process yet.”

Shadow Education Minister Elizabeth Lee wants to know exactly what school services and support will change under the new public schools funding model. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Shadow Education Minister Elizabeth Lee didn’t believe that much more tweaking could be done to the draft budgets.

“[Ms Stephen-Smith] might be talking about the fact that the budgets aren’t finalised [but] what are we doing this week in the chamber? We are literally debating the budget,” she said.

“Schools received their budgets on the 25th of August. It’s been a month, so it’s all good for her to say that she’s been talking to schools and she’ll talk to them about what’s happening, but the principals and the teachers and parents have told us that they have no more clarity a month on.”

Despite what’s being said at a political level, public school families remain confused about how the changes will affect their school.

ACT Parents executive officer Veronica Elliott said parents and carers understood the need for more equity across the system, but it wasn’t clear whether funding was really going where it’s needed most.

“For school communities, they’ve got lots of questions. They want to be able to see how their school compares across the system, what are the funding differences, why are some schools getting more money than others, and I think at this stage that’s still a bit unclear,” she said.

“We’re concerned that principals are having to make decisions now … when the system hasn’t really decided what should be a core education provision.

“We’re potentially putting the cart before the horse.”

Ms Elliott said regardless of whether a school was losing or gaining money, the justifications needed to be made public.

“It’s on the government to show that actually what they’re putting forward does actually send the money where it is most needed,” she said.

Canberra’s public schools will be shut until 10.30 am on Thursday, 24 September, due to industrial action.

canberra.title: High-flying RAAF reconnaissance aircraft achieve an initial operating capability
canberra.snippet: The Royal Australian Air Force has declared an initial operational capability (IOC) for two of the world’s most advanced reconnaissance a...
canberra.content:
RAAF MQ-4C Triton, P-8A Poseidon, and MC-55A Peregrine aircraft on the ramp at RAAF Tindal. Photo: ADF.

The Royal Australian Air Force has declared an initial operational capability (IOC) for two of the world’s most advanced reconnaissance aircraft.

At a media conference at Edinburgh near Adelaide on Tuesday (22 September), Defence Minister Richard Marles and Chief of Air Force Air Marshal Stephen Chappell said the Gulfstream/L3Harris MC-55A Peregrine and the uncrewed Northrop Grumman MQ-4C Triton had been declared operational.

The declaration of IOC usually comes after a minimum number of aircraft have been delivered, sufficient maintenance and aircrews are in place, aircrew and maintenance training is able to be conducted in Australia, and the aircraft and systems have successfully been deployed and demonstrated their ability to conduct operational missions.

The MC-55A has been ‘seen’ on flight tracker apps in recent weeks conducting electronic intelligence (ELINT) missions around the Philippines and South China Sea where China has asserted its sovereignty over parts of the region in the past decade, none of which is recognised by neighbouring countries nor the United Nations.

Converted from the Gulfstream G550 corporate jet, the MC-55A features several distended bulges and apertures including a long ‘canoe’ fairing under the forward fuselage, numerous other small antennae all around the airframe, and a retractable electro optical/infrared (EO/IR) camera.

The Peregrine has a passive high-altitude, long-range electronic intelligence role, gathering data on adversary land-based, naval and airborne radar and communications systems.

The data gleaned by the aircraft’s onboard systems can be transmitted in real-time, and can be compiled into a data library for Australian and allied combat aircraft so they can better identify, classify, and possibly disrupt these systems if deemed a threat.

The RAAF has ordered four MC-55As, the first of which arrived in Australia in January, and three of which have now been delivered to No. 10 Squadron based at Edinburgh.

The first of four MQ-4C Triton uncrewed maritime surveillance aircraft was delivered to Australia in June 2024, and three aircraft are now in service.

The aircraft themselves along with a combined Air Force and industry maintenance and ground support team are based at RAAF Base Tindal in the Northern Territory, while the pilots, sensor operators and the operating No. 9 Squadron headquarters are located at Edinburgh.

Chief of Air Force AIRMSHL Stephen Chappell talks to media in front of a P-8A (left) and MC-55A at Edinburgh. Photo: ADF.

Being an uncrewed aircraft the size of a 737, the Triton will rarely overfly populated areas, although a much-delayed sense and avoid (SAA) radar is planned to be installed and certified to allow it to operate in controlled airspace in the future.

Based on the Global Hawk, the Triton’s long glider-like wings allow it to fly at altitudes above 55,000 feet for more than 24 hours, giving it the ability to cover vast swathes of ocean in a single mission.

For the maritime role, the Triton has a strengthened airframe, de-icing on the wings and engine inlet, a powerful MFAS radar, maritime modes for the MTS-B EO/IR sensor, and a comprehensive MULTI-INT electronic intelligence system able to listen to and categorise adversary electronic emissions.

Complementing the Peregrine and Triton milestones was the arrival in Australia of the RAAF’s 14th and final P-8A Poseidon maritime response aircraft, the return of the first Poseidon to be upgraded to the enhanced Increment 3 Block 2 configuration, and the commencement of work in Australia to upgrade the remainder of the fleet.

Mr Marles said the milestones demonstrated the government’s commitment to the RAAF’s air intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities.

“South Australia is central to this effort,” he said.

“RAAF Base Edinburgh is becoming one of the most important hubs for advanced Defence capability in the country, supporting our national security and highly skilled Australian jobs.

“The government is investing approximately $5.5 billion over the decade to continue to enhance the ADF’s air intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance and maritime patrol and response capabilities that will create additional opportunities for Australian industry well into the future.”

AIRMSHL Chappell added, “Our people have been at the heart of delivering the air intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capability for Australia, demonstrating exceptional skill, professionalism and dedication in bringing these complex systems into service.

“I congratulate our whole Air Domain team, from across industry, the public service and Air Force for their exceptional work to deliver these cutting edge capabilities for Australia.

“The achievements announced today mark a significant step forward in Air Force capability, delivering persistent, long-range maritime surveillance that strengthens our ability to protect Australia’s interests and deliver highly effective air power as part of the integrated, focused force.”

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

canberra.title: Smiles at UN belie stark differences over algorithms and AI
canberra.snippet: Anthony Albanese and Donald Trump have met for a quick selfie on the sidelines of a United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York...
canberra.content:
US President Donald Trump and Australian PM Anthony Albanese take a selfie at the UN. Photo: Anthony Albanese Facebook.

Anthony Albanese and Donald Trump have met for a quick selfie on the sidelines of a United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York, but the smiling faces of the Australian Prime Minister and the US President give no hint of their disagreement over the PM’s digital duty of care legislation.

Late on Tuesday (22 September, Australian time), the US Government made an unusual public intervention in Australia’s political debate over reining in tech companies and allowing social media users to opt out of algorithm feeds.

The Trump Administration expressed “serious concerns” over Labor’s digital duty of care bill and described it as an “extraterritorial censorship of protected speech”.

It said US social media companies should be excluded from the policy.

The public statement was made in response to a consultation on the bill, which the US Embassy in Canberra posted on its website.

“The large majority of social media and video-sharing platforms that would be affected are US-headquartered companies, operating substantially on US soil and serving American users alongside Australian ones,” the statement said.

“We ask that Australia withdraw any plans to mandate that platforms algorithmically suppress content based on ambiguous government-defined safety criteria … The US government has made clear its opposition to foreign measures that result in extraterritorial censorship of protected speech by Americans online.”

President Trump’s subsequent speech also made it clear he did not want further regulations to stifle the development and rollout of artificial intelligence.

Before meeting with Mr Trump, the PM said he listened “respectfully” to the speech and was looking forward to catching up with him at a reception the President was hosting.

“I look forward to engaging with him there. We have put forward a strong position,” the Prime Minister said.

“I’m proud of what we have done on social media, and the fact that the European Union have now announced a major reform as well, joining the more than 20 countries who’ve taken action – Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, in our own region, New Zealand have now moved.

“And increasingly there’s a recognition that new technology can bring enormous benefits. And artificial intelligence can boost our economy; it can boost productivity; it can advance healthcare in ways that were unimaginable a while ago, with breakthroughs.

“There are a range of advantages, but we need to make sure that humans are in control.”

Asked if he was disappointed at Mr Trump’s dismissal of the middle powers’ statement calling for international guardrails for AI, the PM said he would wait to see what comes from the meeting between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the issue.

“It’s good that they’re meeting and it’s good that this is on the agenda,” he said.

Mr Albanese was also asked if he thought the US Administration had undermined Australia’s position on algorithms.

“Not at all,” the PM said.

“The fact is that we have released an exposure draft of legislation. We haven’t even introduced the legislation before the parliament. We’ll engage constructively.

“I hope the whole of parliament supports it. This should not be a partisan issue.”

The Prime Minister might be wishcasting on that point, as the Coalition has already described the bill as “political censorship”.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said on Wednesday that the bill was not in Australia’s national interest.

“We should always do what’s in our national interest regardless of what anyone else says we should do,” Mr Taylor said.

“It’s not in our national interest to give a blank check to the minister on political censorship, which is what the bill does right now.

“This government always seems to know what is best for all Australians, and it is going to tell us what we are allowed to see on our social media. The minister will decide. That is what this bill allows. That is not appropriate, and we will not support a blank cheque on political censorship.”

The Greens, however, are outraged at the US intervention.

Communications spokesperson Sarah Hanson-Young said the Federal Government should reject it.

“Donald Trump is not our President and big tech are not our masters. Australians will not cop being bullied by Mr Trump and his tech bro mates,” Senator Hanson-Young said.

“The intervention of the Trump Administration into a domestic political debate in Australia is an extraordinary act of foreign interference and the Albanese Government needs to immediately reject it.

“Australians get to decide the laws of our country and how we protect our citizens from harm. For a foreign government to try to tell us what laws we can pass in our sovereign nation is an incredible overreach.

“Mr Trump might be used to trashing reason and convention in his own country, but we will not stand for the US trying to muscle in on Australian domestic policy.

“The Australian parliament cannot be lectured on political censorship by a man who is locking journalists out when they do their job of holding him to account.”

The PM posted the selfie of himself and the President to social media, with the caption “Always good to catch up with @potus”.

canberra.title: Police targeting hoons issue 76 fines, seize three vehicles
canberra.snippet: A police crackdown on hoon drivers destroying the roads on Canberra’s outskirts has resulted in dozens of fines and several vehicle...
canberra.content:
23 September 2026

23 September 2026

An operation focusing on hooning drivers over 18-19 September 2026 resulted in police seizing three vehicles. Photo: ACT Policing.

A police crackdown on hoon drivers destroying the roads on Canberra’s outskirts has resulted in dozens of fines and several vehicles being seized.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said a police operation targetted dangerous drivers in the Territory’s rural areas over Friday and Saturday nights (18-19 September).

As a result, officers issued 76 fines, 45 defect notices and seized three vehicles for improper use.

In addition, police allegedly detected two drink drivers and five drug drivers.

“One man was arrested for an outstanding warrant while another man, who was subject to bail conditions, was charged with driving while disqualified and possessing an offensive weapon,” the police spokesperson said.

Officer in Charge of Road Policing, Detective Inspector Mark Steel, said the operation put a spotlight on the issue of hoon driving.

“You’ve only got to drive along some of our rural roads to see the aftermath of some of this activity, which is totally unacceptable to our rural communities,” he said.

“Large gatherings of people in rural areas late at night presents a significant risk to community safety, and we have a zero tolerance for those who engage in dangerous driving and anti-social behaviour.

“We will continue proactive patrols and enforcement activities.”

australia.title: A ‘grubby rumour’ and a $5m extortion attempt: former Toplace executive gives Icac evidence
australia.snippet: Sharangan Maheswaran also told inquiry his bid for story on unsubstantiated rumour about then-Liberal minister David Elliott was ‘not a s...
australia.content:
A purported $5m extortion attempt of fugitive property developer Jean Nassif was actually a genuine request for his company Toplace to pay a contractor, a lawyer assisting the New South Wales anti-corruption watchdog has argued.

Former Toplace lawyer and executive Sharangan Maheswaran told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Wednesday he had not “dishonestly conveyed” to the building commissioner, David Chandler, that someone had attempted to extort Nassif on Chandler’s behalf.

Icac is investigating the allegation that Liberal figures Christian Ellis, Jeremy Greenwood and Charles Perrottet took $2m in illegal donations from Nassif or Toplace in exchange for political outcomes.

Greenwood and Perrottet have denied payments were for political outcomes. Ellis has moved overseas and is not expected to give evidence. Nassif, in an appearance from his Beirut bedroom, insisted he was “not corrupt”. Maheswaran, who is named in a separate allegation by Icac, has denied any wrongdoing.

The alleged outcomes include damage to the political career of Liberal minister, David Elliott, who had opposed Toplace developments, and the removal of the building commissioner, David Chandler, who had been scrutinising defects in Toplace apartments.

The commission has previously heard that Nassif claimed two individuals had asked him for $5m on Chandler’s behalf to lift prohibition orders on Toplace developments. Maheswaran subsequently passed on details of the alleged extortion attempt to Charles Perrottet.

Chandler is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.

On Wednesday, the commission heard a phone call recorded by Nassif with one of the alleged individuals, contractor Navid Ardestani, who is not named in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.

“Navid mate,” Nassif began the call. “I didn’t know you were so fucking powerful, mate”, he continued, accusing Ardestani of sending a “report” to the building commissioner. Earlier on Wednesday, the commission heard that Nassif had become suspicious of Toplace contractors after a report about apartment defects had been passed on to Chandler.

In the call, Ardestani responded, “which report you talking about, sir?”, subsequently requesting a face-to-face meeting with Nassif.

“You can’t see me. You’re a fucking lying cunt. Bye,” Nassif ended the call.

Maheswaran was taken to messages between Ardestani and Nassif after a subsequent meeting between the two men, in which Ardestani wrote that “purpose of this meeting was to get my mate, the builder, to come and fix the issues that the building commissioner requested to be fixed”.

Maheswaran accepted counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer’s suggestion there was “nothing threatening about that”. She put it to him that this was “clearly a request for payment so that remediation works can take place on Jean Nassif’s building”.

He rejected this, saying it was inconsistent with an audio recording of the meeting, which the commission is expected to hear on Thursday.

The commission heard that Maheswaran had already met with Chandler about the alleged extortion attempt, with the building commissioner suggesting they go to the police. Chandler himself subsequently reported it to his departmental head, and was cleared by an internal audit.

Asked why he did not share details of the people allegedly involved in the extortion attempt with Chandler, Maheswaran said he did not think it was relevant.

“Mr Nassif was taking this very, very seriously, was contemplating paying $5m to these people and from my perspective this was obviously not something that was real.”

“The best way to dispel that illusion in Mr Nassif’s mind [was] to raise it with the commissioner with whom we had a good relationship”.

Dwyer later said: “I’m suggesting to you, I want to put it straight, that you dishonestly conveyed to Mr Chandler that there had been a genuine extortion or shakedown attempt from an anonymous person,” he said.

“I absolutely deny that,” said Maheswaran.

A ‘grubby rumour’

On Wednesday morning, Maheswaran accepted he had given a private investigator, “Mr Nanetti”, Elliott’s address in 2020 to investigate a rumour that the MP was breaching Covid-19 restrictions to conduct an extramarital affair. Maheswaran accepted he now knew the rumour to be untrue.

In a statement and evidence to the commission, Elliott has strongly rejected the allegation of an extramarital affair or breach of Covid-19 restrictions. Multiple witnesses have accepted there was no evidence for the allegation.

He said Nanetti initially made “observations” at Elliott’s address as a favour, but he subsequently paid him $1,000 to return to Elliott’s address, where he took photographs.

Dwyer asked him if he had offered Greenwood $1,000 to place a story with a journalist.

Maheswaran said he had, but told the commission it was “not a serious offer”. Dwyer took him to the messages: “You say: ‘1000 bucks if you can get the yarn up’, and Greenwood says ‘Hahaha’, and you reply, ‘Not joking!’”.

The commission heard the men unsuccessfully tried to place the story with the Daily Telegraph, including providing photos of Elliott in a car with a woman who was not his wife and a draft statutory declaration by the private investigator. Elliott has said photographs show him signing documents for work purposes.

Dwyer, who described the story as a “grubby rumour” to which there was no truth, suggested that Maheswaran was “persistent” because he was pursuing a political outcome sought by Nassif.

Maheswaran rejected that, saying he had a “decade of track record pitching stories that are adverse to Liberal National MPs, ministers”. He said Nassif was the source of the rumour about Elliott, but had not requested the story be placed.

Maheswaran is expected to continue giving evidence to the commission on Thursday and Friday. He is the final scheduled witness across nine weeks of public hearings.

Icac’s inquiry continues.

australia.title: Shoebridge says US submission on online safety laws an ‘extraordinary intervention’ – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Andrew Bragg , the shadow housing minister, said he ...
australia.content:
Shoebridge accuses US of overreach in Australia’s online safety laws

The Greens senator David Shoebridge has accused the United States of interfering in Australia’s domestic politics after the Trump administration criticised the government’s proposed opt-in algorithm reforms.

In a submission overnight, the Trump administration warned the measures risked becoming a mechanism for “viewpoint-based censorship” and called for American platforms to be exempted.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Shoebridge said:

It’s an extraordinary intervention in our domestic politics, that’s what we have seen.

The US embassy issuing, basically, a slap down to the Australian government on a piece of domestic legislation that the Australian parliament should be deciding on, not Washington.

It is almost unprecedented in my experience to see a foreign government in this country through their embassy … so overtly try and dissuade the Australian parliament from taking actions to protect the Australian public.

Shoebridge said the US “needs to be brought to heel by the rest of the world” as global discussions continue over artificial intelligence safeguards and the power of major technology companies.

Most services have now been restored. Some business customers are continuing to experience login issues via NAB Connect, and we’re working as quickly as possible to resolve the remaining impacts.

NAB customers report online banking outage

National Australia Bank (NAB) customers are reporting an outage affecting access to the bank’s online services.

According to DownDetector, reports began at about 1pm, peaking at more than 2,000 reports at about 3.30pm.

Users have taken to social media to say they are unable to access their accounts.

NAB has been contacted for comment.

‘Chaos, confusion’: cop recalls jumping castle tragedy

A veteran police officer has described the chaos and mistakes that followed a deadly school jumping castle tragedy, saying unclear chains of command created confusion, AAP reports.

An inquest which began on Monday is examining the circumstances of the tragedy, safety processes and whether there were any departmental deficiencies.

Tasmania Police constable Dean Wotherspoon was one of the first officers to attend the Hillcrest primary school accident on 16 December 2021.

Students Addison Stewart, Chace Harrison, Jye Sheehan, Jalailah Jayne-Maree Jones, Peter Dodt and Zane Mellor died after a freak “dust devil” wind gust lifted the jumping castle into the air above the Devonport school grounds.

The leading forensic officer told an inquest on Wednesday:

I think the phrase perhaps is organised chaos.

There were a lot of people doing their utmost to save children.

Police officers, school staff, paramedics all doing what they could. It was nothing like I had seen.

Rosemary Gamble, the operator of Taz-Zorb, which set up the inflatable equipment, was in 2025 cleared of criminal workplace safety breaches.

Achol Arok

Good afternoon!

I hope today has been nice to you. I’ll be here to take you through the rest of the day’s news.

Ima Caldwell

That’s all from me today folks.

The blog is now in the capable hands of Achol Arok.

See you next time!

Inner west council to ban AI smartglasses in public facilities

Sydney’s inner west council has moved to ban smartglasses and other wearable recording devices in its facilities, including pools, change rooms, childcare centres and public toilets.

Inner west councillor Kerrie Fergusson said that the technology is likely “just the beginning of many new challenges for local councils”.

For people with vision or hearing impairments, they offer a new level of independence. But they can also discreetly record high-definition video and live-stream, creating genuine privacy concerns …

This isn’t tearing down new technology like a bunch of 19th-century luddites, but ensuring AI technology properly serves our community without compromising its privacy or civil liberties.

Council staff have been asked to report back on how the ban will be implemented, including conditions of entry and signage requirements.

Exemptions will be provided to people who rely on the technology as accessibility devices.

As reported earlier this morning, smartglasses could soon be banned across Sydney’s eastern suburbs beaches Coogee, Clovelly and Maroubra under a motion put forward to Randwick council. It has already banned the technology at the Des Renford leisure centre, citing “growing community concerns” about their potential misuse.

It also follows City of Sydney councillors voting to ban smartglasses at council gyms, childcare centres and pools on Monday.

Police appeal for information after Wagyu cow ‘unlawfully’ shot and butchered in Queensland

Detectives from Queensland’s Rural and Stock Crime Squad are appealing for public information, after a Wagyu cow was “unlawfully shot and butchered for meat” on a property in Queensland.

Police believe trespassers entered the property in Farnborough on 13 or 14 June.

Investigators urge anyone who noticed suspicious activity or captured dashcam footage along Fishing Creek Road, off Farnborough Road, between 13 and 16 June to contact police or Crime Stoppers.

Parenting advocate Georgie Dent tells National Press Club that Australians should get 52 weeks paid parental leave

More on the national press club address today by Georgie Dent, Parenthood chief executive …

Dent cited Treasury data showing that having children reduces the earnings of Australian women by an average of 55% over the first five years of parenthood.

Dent said families need two incomes to stay afloat in the current economy and even with both parents working, they have less breathing room in their household budget.

For many families it feels like a cruel game of whack-a-mole …

For parents of young children seeking to raise and provide for their family one obstacle towers over the others: early childhood education and care.

Too many face an impossible bind. They cannot access it, they cannot afford it, or they cannot trust what is available. This isn’t perceived: the options families have are largely determined by what the market has delivered.

Dent will call for a policy pathway from government for the provision of 52 weeks of paid parental leave, up from 26 weeks currently paid for by taxpayers, and meaningful parental leave for fathers and partners.

The speech comes after Monday’s intergenerational report showed that, for the first time, more Australians will be dying than being born in 40 years’ time.

Read more here:

Press Club says it will never ban journalists from ‘doing their job’

The host of today’s national press club momentarily interrupted question time to say it will never ban journalists from “doing their job”.

Just another message, we’re going to depart for our theme for a second.

[There is] a lot of news at the moment, and in recent months, about journalists not being able to, you know, attend press conferences, et cetera.

Just a note on behalf of the national press club that no journalists will ever be banned from doing their job here.

The message was greeted by applause, before returning to the topic of childcare costs.

This press club comment comes after US president Donald Trump banned journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House.

In Australia, the ABC and the Guardian have called on One Nation to reverse its ban on select media outlets from press conferences amid warnings the party is practising censorship and actively avoiding public scrutiny. Journalist Peter Greste has written for Guardian Australia about how these circumstances show “why Australia urgently needs a media freedom bill”:

Anthony Albanese meets Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi in New York

Tom McIlroy

Anthony Albanese has met Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, at the United Nations – the first time the pair have been together since Albanese’s comments about melons in a controversial podcast.

The PM has repeatedly rejected suggestions he made offensive comments about a gift of two melons from Takaichi on the Bush Deep podcast in early July. Japan’s ambassador to Australia downplayed any possible offence and said Tokyo had been reassured by the Australian government that Albanese’s comments had been misunderstood.

Albanese wrote on social media, in a post that included a photo with world leaders including Takaichi:

Working with our international partners. Standing up for Australian interests. Finding global solutions to global challenges.

Australia’s voice matters at the United Nations. And it’s here that we’re delivering for Australians back home.

While in New York, Albanese has met Britain’s Andy Burnham, the French president Emmanuel Macron, Pedro Sanchez of Spain and the US president Donald Trump.

Plan to shift $4bn of NDIS spending snagging on lone holdout state

Health minister Mark Butler says he is frustrated that Queensland is the only state or territory not to sign up to the government’s Thriving Kids program, a week before the first phase is due to begin.

The health minister told ABC Radio on Wednesday:

I’m a little frustrated they haven’t signed because all other states and territories, Liberal and Labor alike, CLP government in the NT has signed on.

The Queensland premier, David Crisafulli, was shirking a responsibility he had previously promised to accept, according to Butler. He said:

I can’t imagine a Queensland government that, for the next 15 months, would sit on its hands and pretend it does not have a very serious obligation to follow the rest of the country.

Frankly [it should] implement commitments that the premier made at the national cabinet meeting earlier this year.

Gus Lamont’s parents make teary plea for information about missing boy

Tory Shepherd

Gus’s parents, Josh Lamont and Jess Murray, have spoken in a video shown by police.

Williams said Gus was “learning so much and had such a bright future ahead of him”:

He should have celebrated his fifth birthday and his little brother’s first birthday with us.

Lamont thanked family, friends, the community and those who were part of the search for Gus, and said:

We believe someone knows something. Someone knows what happened to Gus. Someone knows where he is.

Fielke emphasised that neither of them are suspects and vowed to keep searching for answers.

Police offer $1m reward for information about missing boy Gus Lamont

Tory Shepherd

A $1m reward for information about missing four-year-old Gus Lamont is on offer, as police say they have found no evidence to suggest he is still alive.

It has been almost a year since four-year-old Gus went missing from his family’s enormous sheep farm in the South Australian outback.

He was last seen playing outside at 5pm on Saturday 27 September. Half an hour later, he was gone.

His disappearance sparked one of the biggest searches the state has ever undertaken, with new searches launched as new information or theories came to light.

Volunteers, police, emergency service and defence personnel, along with dogs and divers and drones scoured the 60,000 hectare Oak Park Station, about 300km inland from Adelaide.

One of the biggest moments in the saga came in February this year, when the South Australian police declared his disappearance a major crime, and said they had identified a suspect.

Det Supt Darren Fielke said at the time they had effectively ruled out Gus wandering off or being abducted, and that they were now investigating someone in his household.

The suspect was not one of his parents, Fielke said.

The SA premier, Peter Malinauskas, said they stand ready to do “everything they can” to help police. He said it would go to anyone who had information leading to a body or a conviction. He said it was a “crystal clear” message:

If you know something you’ve gotta speak.

The disappearance of Gus Lamont has deeply shocked and saddened all South Australians. I cannot imagine the anguish that Gus’s parents Jess and Josh are going through, and my thoughts remain with them.

Fielke said the police would do everything they could “to locate Gus and reunite him with his family”.

Police arrest Melbourne man who allegedly pledged allegiance to Isis

Counter-terrorism police have arrested a Melbourne man, who they allege acted as an Isis propagandist.

The 65-year-old was arrested during a raid of a home in Carlton this morning.

Police allege he pledged allegiance to Isis and has played a significant role in spreading propaganda for the terrorist group, sending about 10,000 files of violent extremist material.

The man is alleged to have shared information about avoiding detection from authorities and instructions on how to plan and conduct mass casualty attacks.

AFP acting assistant commissioner counter-terrorism, Paula Hudson, spoke to reporters just after midday.

We will allege the videos, photographs, audio files and documents contain messages relating to current content, being executions, mass murder, torture and propaganda ….

Let me be clear, terrorist propaganda is not harmless online content. Terrorist organisations like Isis rely on online platforms to distribute propaganda and recruit supporters.

Hudson added that police launched an investigation after Australian Border Force officers found suspicious material on electronic devices seized as the man flew out of Melbourne.

She said the man was a “principal distributor of Isis propaganda within the group”.

The man lives with his wife and is an Australian citizen, according to police.

australia.title: Gus Lamont’s parents make emotional plea as $1m reward offered for information about disappearance
australia.snippet: No trace of Gus has been found since he went missing from his family’s South Australian farm on 27 September last year The parents of mis...
australia.content:
The parents of missing four-year-old Gus Lamont have made an emotional plea for any information about their “unique little boy” as authorities offered a $1m reward over the disappearance.

No trace of Gus has been found since he went missing from his family’s enormous sheep farm in the South Australian outback almost a year ago.

Gus’s parents, Joshua Lamont and Jessica Murray, pleaded with the public to come forward with any information, no matter how small.

It had been “the most devastating and inexplicable event we have ever experienced”, Murray said in a video message released on Wednesday.

“Our memories of Gus are of a beautiful, sweet and unique little boy who loved music, listening to stories, and playing in the natural world.

“During the time Gus has been missing, he should have celebrated his fifth birthday and his little brother’s first birthday with us.”

A tearful Lamont said they were desperate for answers.

“We believe that someone knows something. Someone knows what happened to Gus, and may even know where he is,” he said.

South Australian police Det Supt Darren Fielke described the 11 painstaking ground searches in inhospitable territory, which have so far turned up no useful clues – although some “anomalies” in aerial images may prompt yet another search.

Officials are hoping the state government reward of up to $1m for anyone with information leading to a conviction or a body will help move the investigation forwards.

Gus, described as both shy and adventurous, was last seen playing outside at 5pm on Saturday 27 September. Half an hour later, when his family went to check on him, he was gone.

His disappearance sparked one of the biggest searches the state has ever undertaken, with new searches launched as new information or theories came to light.

Volunteers, police, emergency services and defence personnel, along with dogs, divers and drones, aircraft and Aboriginal trackers scoured the 60,000 hectare Oak Park station, about 300km inland from Adelaide.

One of the biggest moments in the search came in February this year, when South Australia police declared his disappearance a major crime, and said they had identified a suspect.

Fielke said at the time they had effectively ruled out Gus wandering off or being abducted, and that they were now investigating someone in his household.

The suspect was not one of his parents, Fielke said, something he emphasised on Wednesday.

Fielke said Task Force Horizon had covered more than 700 sq km and undertaken “a painstaking, methodical, forensically detailed manual search of the aerial imagery”, which “identified some anomalies”. Those anomalies will be reviewed before any decision to start a new search is made.

The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, said there had been “no sign of Gus”, so the government was offering the $1m reward in hope of solving the case.

Previous state governments have offered the same amount in cases of missing children, including the three Beaumont children who disappeared without a trace from an Adelaide beach in 1966.

“We put this in place because … we spare no expense. Justice needs to be done here one way or another,” Malinauskas said.

“We will not tolerate, as a state, any circumstances where children go missing and are not able to be accounted for.”

Anyone with information relating to the disappearance of Gus Lamont was urged to contact crime stoppers.

“We’re going to continue to thoroughly and meticulously investigate the disappearance of Gus until we get a resolution,” Fielke said.

australia.title: Jesse Baird ‘petrified’ of Beau Lamarre-Condon and kept repeating ‘he has a gun’, court hears
australia.snippet: Friend sobs in witness box and tells Sydney murder trial Baird was scared to go to the police Follow our Australia news live blog for lat...
australia.content:
Before he was fatally shot, Jesse Baird became “petrified” of Beau Lamarre and kept repeating that the police officer had a gun, a court has heard.

Lamarre-Condon has been accused of fatally shooting Sydney couple Jesse Baird, 26, and Luke Davies, 29, with a police service weapon at Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.

The 31-year-old pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

Lamarre-Condon developed an “obsession and infatuation” with Baird, which manifested in compulsive actions during their brief relationship, the prosecution alleged.

By the time Baird decided he wanted to end things in November 2023, the behaviour had escalated.

Corey-Dean Thorpe, who had previously been in a years-long relationship with the 26-year-old and remained close friends, began sobbing in the witness box as he told the trial how Baird felt.

“He was petrified,” Thorpe told the New South Wales supreme court.

“I’d never heard him so scared in his voice before.

“He just kept repeating, ‘he has a gun’.”

Baird told Thorpe he was “extremely scared” of Lamarre-Condon because he had a gun and was a member of the police force, the court heard.

Asked by crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC if the 26-year-old had said he was scared to go to the police because Lamarre-Condon was a police officer, Thorpe agreed.

Baird was also worried Lamarre-Condon would make a false allegation against him that would “ruin his career”, Thorpe said.

Because he was a television presenter on children’s show Totally Wild and an AFL umpire, he needed a certification to work with children, the court heard.

During their relationship, Baird told Thorpe that Lamarre-Condon would go through his phone when he was asleep, find other men Baird had been talking to, and block their numbers before deleting their chats.

Lamarre-Condon would also use his own close friends story on Instagram to target “romantic rivals”, the prosecution alleged.

Damon Wilson, who had been casually seeing Baird, told the court about an incident in November 2023 when the TV presenter had to go to Melbourne for work.

Lamarre-Condon added Wilson to his close friends story on Instagram before posting a photo of a bouquet captioned “when he’s in Melbourne but still sends you these” with a heart-eyes emoji.

Baird later told his work colleague Briony Blackstone that he had not sent Lamarre-Condon any flowers, the court heard.

He found out the police officer had created a close friends list that included only one person so Lamarre-Condon could imply he and Baird were in a more serious relationship, Blackstone told the court.

This wasn’t the first time he had done this, the prosecution alleged.

Earlier in 2023, Lamarre-Condon had told his work colleague Rubina Shrestha that he had created a close friends group which had only one person: a Canberra man who had been seeing Baird.

He then posted a photo of Baird or himself with Baird to “send out a message that they’re together and Jesse’s not available,” Shrestha told the court.

When he told her about the bouquet close friends story, Shrestha told him: “that’s crazy” before Lamarre-Condon replied, “it works”.

After seeing the flowers in Lamarre-Condon’s story, Wilson messaged Baird, who confirmed he was not in a relationship with Lamarre-Condon.

Wilson said to Baird in a message: “I was a little confused why he added me to his close friends as soon as we met then starting posting photos of you guys … you getting him flowers. Glad we are on the same page.”

A week later Wilson received a protracted message from Lamarre-Condon warning him about Baird’s supposed “gaslighting”.

“He literally destroyed me,” Lamarre-Condon said in messages read to the court.

“It took me so long to recover from all the manipulation.

“He has tried to make me look like the bad guy.”

Around this time, Baird asked Thorpe for advice on how to break up with Lamarre-Condon.

Baird told Thorpe he was worried about what would happen when he ended things “because of the gun and because the accused had stalked and controlled him”, the prosecutor alleged.

But he pushed ahead with the break-up and confronted Lamarre-Condon about the flowers in the close friends story.

The officer responded by claiming the flowers were sent by his stepdad, who was living in Melbourne, to his mother, the court heard.

Lamarre-Condon later told his colleague Shrestha he “would do anything to get him back”.

On 3 February 2024, months after the break-up, one of Baird’s best friends, Matthew Edwards, asked if he had heard from Lamarre-Condon.

Edwards said Baird had replied: “No, thank fuck, I’m so done with him.”

“Once I move house, this will be the last piece of me that Beau knows.”

Baird confirmed his new relationship with Davies to Edwards soon after during their last phone call together.

“He was almost falling in love with him,” Edwards told the court.

“I’d never seen Jesse as happy with Luke as what I’d seen him ever. There was something about Luke that just lit Jesse up: they were the real deal.”

Lamarre-Condon’s defence team has claimed the police officer was acting in self-defence when he disguised himself as an Uber Eats driver and entered Baird’s home on 19 February.

Defence lawyer John Stratton SC argued a struggle had ensued which led to the shots that killed Davies and Baird.

The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues.
